blocks.text: We’ll now move from the general interpretation framework to **actual high-yield X-ray patterns you should be able to recognise almost immediately in an OSCE**.
“You are shown a chest X-ray of a child. Interpret the X-ray.”
“This is a paediatric chest radiograph. I would first confirm the patient's identity, date and the projection.”
Trachea is central and the carina is appropriately positioned.
Both lung fields are clear and symmetrically aerated with no focal consolidation, collapse or pleural effusion.

content_groups.group_title: AP films can make the heart appear artificially enlarged.

blocks.text: Both hemidiaphragms are intact and the costophrenic angles are clear.

“This is a paediatric chest radiograph. The film is adequately exposed with no significant rotation. The trachea is central. Both lungs are clear and symmetrically expanded with no focal air-space opacity, collapse or pleural effusion. The cardiac silhouette is not enlarged. The diaphragms and costophrenic angles are clear. There is no acute bony abnormality. Overall, this is an essentially normal chest radiograph.”
One of the **most important paediatric chest X-ray findings**.
A region of the lung becomes **whiter than normal**.
“There is a focal air-space opacity involving the right lower zone with air bronchograms.”

content_groups.group_title: dark branching air-filled bronchi against a white consolidated lung.

blocks.text: “There is focal air-space consolidation in the right lower lobe with visible air bronchograms. There is no significant pleural effusion. The appearances are most consistent with right lower lobe pneumonia.”
**Q: What causes consolidation in a child?**
**Consolidation = increased opacity + air bronchograms ± silhouette sign.**

items.text: Mediastinal shift towards the affected side

blocks.text: “There is increased opacity involving the right upper lobe with associated volume loss and elevation of the minor fissure, consistent with right upper lobe collapse.”

content_groups.group_title: Visible pleural line with absence of peripheral lung markings beyond it.

blocks.text: You may see a black area at the periphery.

“There is a right-sided pneumothorax demonstrated by a visible visceral pleural line with absence of peripheral lung markings. There is associated mediastinal shift to the left, suggesting tension physiology.”
**Q: What makes it a tension pneumothorax?**
“Evidence of significant pressure effect, particularly mediastinal shift away from the affected side, in the appropriate clinical context.”
If the child is **clinically unstable with suspected tension pneumothorax**, do not wait for an X-ray before emergency decompression.

items.text: Large effusion may obscure the diaphragm
Massive effusion may cause mediastinal shift away

blocks.text: “There is homogeneous opacity involving the right lower hemithorax with blunting of the right costophrenic angle and a meniscus sign, consistent with a right pleural effusion.”
A very common paediatric OSCE scenario.

blocks.title: Often **not routinely required clinically**, but if shown:

blocks.text: “The lungs are hyperinflated with bilateral peribronchial/interstitial prominence and mild patchy atelectatic changes. There is no focal lobar consolidation. The appearances are compatible with viral bronchiolitis in the appropriate clinical setting.”
The lungs appear unusually dark and expanded.

“There is bilateral hyperinflation with increased lung volumes and mild peribronchial prominence, without focal consolidation or pleural effusion. The appearances may be seen with reactive airways disease/asthma in the appropriate clinical context.”
**Q: Is a chest X-ray routinely required in uncomplicated asthma?**
“No. Asthma is primarily a clinical diagnosis, and routine chest radiography is not required unless there is concern about an alternative diagnosis or complication.”

content_groups.group_title: Premature baby + respiratory distress + diffuse granular lungs

items.text: Sometimes near-complete white-out in severe disease

blocks.text: “There are low lung volumes with diffuse bilateral fine reticulogranular pulmonary opacification and prominent air bronchograms. In a premature neonate with respiratory distress, these appearances are consistent with neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.”
**Surfactant deficiency → alveolar collapse → reduced compliance → diffuse opacification.**

subsections.subsection_title: 9. TRANSIENT TACHYPNOEA OF THE NEWBORN — TTN

blocks.text: Term or near-term neonate + tachypnoea shortly after birth.

items.text: Hyperinflation or normal/slightly increased lung volume

blocks.text: Normal/high volume + prominent interstitial/perihilar markings + fissural fluid

“There is mild hyperinflation with bilateral perihilar interstitial prominence and fluid within the interlobar fissures, without focal consolidation. In the appropriate neonatal clinical context, the appearances are suggestive of transient tachypnoea of the newborn.”

content_groups.group_title: Term/post-term baby + meconium-stained liquor + respiratory distress

blocks.text: “There are bilateral patchy coarse air-space opacities with areas of hyperinflation and atelectatic change. In the clinical context of a term neonate with meconium exposure, the appearances are compatible with meconium aspiration syndrome.”
“The lungs demonstrate heterogeneous hyperinflation with coarse interstitial and patchy atelectatic changes, compatible with chronic lung disease of prematurity.”
Newborn + severe respiratory distress + scaphoid abdomen.

“There are multiple air-filled bowel loops within the left hemithorax with associated mediastinal shift to the right and reduced aeration of the left lung. The appearances are highly suggestive of a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia.”
**Q: Why should the child not be bag-mask ventilated?**
Air insufflation into the stomach and bowel can worsen thoracic compression.

content_groups.group_title: Immediate endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression.
Why might the foreign body not be visible?

blocks.text: Many foreign bodies are **radiolucent**, particularly organic materials such as nuts.
The affected side may remain expanded because of a **ball-valve effect**.
“There is asymmetric hyperinflation of the right lung with relative increased lucency and reduced vascular markings, raising suspicion of air trapping secondary to an aspirated foreign body.”
This is an **absolute OSCE must-recognise foreign body**.
Round metallic object with a **double-rim/halo appearance**.
Step-off or **bevelled edge** may be seen.

blocks.title: A button battery lodged in the oesophagus can cause:

blocks.text: “This is a radiopaque round foreign body in the oesophagus with a double-rim appearance, highly suspicious for a button battery. This is an emergency requiring urgent specialist assessment and removal.”
This is because of the anatomical orientation of the oesophagus and airway.

rows: Coin usually en face on AP

blocks.text: Little or no distal bowel gas in complete obstruction.

“There are two prominent gas-filled structures in the upper abdomen representing the stomach and proximal duodenum, with absence of distal bowel gas. This produces a classic double-bubble appearance, consistent with complete duodenal obstruction, most likely duodenal atresia.”
Multiple proximal dilated loops, classically producing:
One of the **highest-yield neonatal abdominal X-rays**.

content_groups.group_title: Bubbly or linear lucencies along the bowel wall.

blocks.text: “There is abnormal intramural gas within multiple bowel loops, producing a bubbly/linear appearance consistent with pneumatosis intestinalis. Portal venous gas may also be present. In a preterm neonate, these findings are highly suspicious for necrotising enterocolitis.”
Free air can be more difficult to detect.

items.text: Inner and outer walls of bowel.

blocks.text: Large amount of free abdominal gas may outline the peritoneal cavity.
“There is evidence of free intraperitoneal gas, with gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall, consistent with pneumoperitoneum.”
Paediatric skeletal X-ray is extremely high yield.
The growth plate may appear widened.
“There is widening of the distal radial and ulnar growth plates with metaphyseal cupping, fraying and splaying. The appearances are consistent with rickets.”
The paediatric bone is flexible, so it may fracture on one side while remaining intact on the other.
Cortical break on one side with bending of the opposite cortex.
“There is a cortical break involving one side of the distal radius with angulation but preservation of the opposite cortex, consistent with a greenstick fracture.”
Buckling of the cortex without a complete cortical break.
“There is focal cortical buckling of the distal radial metaphysis without a complete cortical break, consistent with a buckle/torus fracture.”
This is a **major paediatric OSCE favourite**.
Child falls on an outstretched hand.

items.text: Posterior displacement of distal fragment in extension injuries

blocks.text: The anterior humeral line should intersect the middle third of the capitellum.
A supracondylar fracture is not simply a bone injury.
**Types III and IV**, because the articular surface is involved.

subsections.subsection_title: 25. DEVELOPMENTAL DYSPLASIA OF THE HIP — DDH

blocks.text: X-ray is usually more useful after ossification develops; ultrasound is preferred in young infants.
Disruption of **Shenton's line** suggests abnormal femoral head position.
“The femoral head is displaced superolaterally with an abnormal acetabular configuration and disruption of Shenton's line, consistent with developmental dysplasia of the hip.”
A normal early X-ray **does not exclude osteomyelitis**.
MRI is much more sensitive for early disease.

“There is metaphyseal lucency and cortical irregularity with associated periosteal reaction involving the proximal tibia. In the appropriate clinical setting, the findings are suspicious for osteomyelitis.”
This is particularly important in paediatrics.
Certain fracture patterns should raise concern when the history does not fit.

items.text: Multiple fractures at different stages of healing
Unusual fractures in a non-mobile infant

blocks.text: If you have limited revision time, prioritise these:
When the examiner puts **any paediatric X-ray** in front of you and you don't immediately recognise it, don't panic.

content_groups.group_title: ID → TECHNIQUE → SYSTEM → ABNORMALITY → DIAGNOSIS → NEXT

blocks.text: “I would assess the projection, exposure, rotation and adequacy.”
Don't jump immediately to the diagnosis.
“There is focal right lower lobe air-space consolidation with air bronchograms.”
This is where you can gain extra marks.
“In a clinically unstable child with these findings, I would immediately assess and stabilise the airway, breathing and circulation and involve the appropriate paediatric/surgical team.”

content_groups.group_title: ⭐ The golden rule for X-ray OSCEs

blocks.text: **“I see…” → “This suggests…” → “Therefore my diagnosis is…” → “I would…”**
That distinction often separates a safe OSCE answer from a weak one.
